topics.topic: Value that sets the maximum size of each sandbox scratch file
questions: Is each scratch file limited by the release-wide `sandbox_scratch_bytes_max` named in rule 1, or by a missing per-contract ResourceBounds field?
Which value sets the maximum size of each file written in the sandbox exchange directory?
Which numeric limit governs each scratch file, given that M04 contains no scratch-size field while A03 rule 1 and A20 define the separate release constant `sandbox_scratch_bytes_max`?

quotes:
an environment
   holding only `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` (rule 2), a read-only runtime, and one private exchange directory in which every file the code writes is
   bounded by `sandbox_scratch_bytes_max` (rule 5).
judgement.why: A03 explicitly assigns the release-wide sandbox_scratch_bytes_max to every scratch file, so no per-contract field is missing.

topics.topic: Outcome classification for resource-limit and storage-exhaustion events, including caught errors and partial writes
questions: What outcome is recorded when a scratch write fails because host storage or the exchange filesystem is exhausted rather than because the per-file scratch limit was hit, including when the submitted code catches the write error?
Exactly which observable events constitute a memory, process-count, or scratch limit hit, including caught errors and partial writes?

quotes: execute_function: [SECURITY_BOUNDARY] MUST start bubblewrap with new user, PID, IPC, UTS and network namespaces and no network interface but the new namespace's own loopback, which bubblewrap brings up, the environment cleared and then set exactly to the imported SANDBOX_ENVIRONMENT constant, exactly the host paths of the imported SANDBOX_RUNTIME_PATHS constant bound read-only, which hold the release's Python runtime and standard library, inside the new root the symbolic links of the imported SANDBOX_ROOT_SYMLINKS constant (each name linking to its target, made by bubblewrap --symlink; links, not host paths), one fresh private exchange directory bound read-write in which every file the code writes is bounded by the imported RELEASE_CEILING_SANDBOX_SCRATCH_BYTES_MAX constant through the runner's setrlimit file-size limit (the runner ignores SIGXFSZ, so a write past it raises OSError with errno EFBIG, the only scratch hit; ENOSPC or EDQUOT from exhausted host storage is an ordinary raised error, crashed if it escapes run; code that restores SIGXFSZ's default and is killed by it exited abnormally, crashed), the directory as a whole having no separate bound, bubblewrap's own fresh proc and minimal dev mounts, and no other host directory; the child dies with its parent, and the runner is the init of the new PID namespace (bubblewrap --as-pid-1), so bubblewrap exits only after the host kernel has killed and reaped every other process of that namespace. Every descriptor the environment needs from the parent — the write end of the trap channel, the --info-fd pipe — reaches bubblewrap by inheritance, passed with subprocess pass_fds, and bubblewrap keeps it open for the child: bubblewrap has no option that names a descriptor to keep, and --preserve-fds does not exist. The interpreter it starts there is the kernel's own CPython addressed by its resolved path, os.path.realpath(sys.executable), which lies under a path of the imported SANDBOX_RUNTIME_PATHS constant; a launcher path such as a virtual environment's is never bound into the sandbox.

execute_function: [BEHAVIOR] process_count bounds the tasks of the code alive at once: the runner's main thread counts as the first, every live thread and every process the code forked with os.fork counts with its threads, and bubblewrap's own processes are not counted, so process_count 1 allows code without threads or forks. Process creation other than os.fork — subprocess, os.system, os.posix_spawn, os.posix_spawnp and the os.exec family — is subprocess use and raises in the audit hook as a trap hit (A03 rule 4). The runner's audit hook, on os.fork and on starting a thread, counts the tasks of the environment's proc and, when the new task would exceed process_count, writes a resource hit to the channel and raises, so the execution concludes resource_exhausted even when the code catches the error; the runner's limit on the number of processes, process_count + 1, stays the outer bound, and a creation it refuses is reported the same way (A03 required test 2).

execute_function: [BEHAVIOR] A memory, scratch or output bound counts as hit only when the parent observes it from outside — the parent kills an environment for its wall deadline alone, and a process killed by a signal, SIGXFSZ included, exited abnormally: a MemoryError or an OSError with errno EFBIG for a file past the file-size limit escaped run and reached the parent through the exchange channel, or the output count exceeds bounds.output_bytes; code that catches such an error and returns is judged by what it returned, like any other output (owner, 2026-10-06). Only the process bound is also seen inside, because every thread start and os.fork passes the runner's audit hook.

execute_function: [DETERMINISM_OR_ORDERING] The outcome is the first that holds, in this order of = models.SandboxOutcome: timeout when the wall deadline passed; resource_exhausted when the memory, process, scratch or output bound was hit; sandbox_violation when the channel recorded any trap hit, even if the code caught it and returned a conforming dict; crashed when the module failed to load, has no run, raised, or the process exited abnormally; contract_violation when the returned value is not a dict with exactly the output ports, a value output cannot be serialized to canonical JSON, a file output is not bytes, a many output is not a list, or fit_port_value with bounds.output_bytes as size bound does not fit an output to its port; otherwise succeeded. The stored value ceiling and the spool ceilings are not the sandbox's: the module that stores or spools an output applies them after the execution has otherwise succeeded.
judgement.why: The later sandbox notes define the observable limit-hit events, caught-error behavior, host-storage failures, signal exits, process refusals and their outcome precedence.
